summary.oneLiner: Aether leveraged geopolitical disruptions to drive >20% pricing gains in its Large-Scale Manufacturing vertical while successfully transitioning toward a high-margin CRAMS/CEM model (55% of revenue) with Site 5 commissioning imminent. Despite Q4 one-offs (fire provision, lack of insurance claim income), the structural shift to complex chemistry and expanded R&D capacity positions the firm for sustained 29-30% EBITDA margins and triple-digit growth in semiconductor materials by 2030.
summary.business: Aether develops, scales up and manufactures advanced intermediates and specialty chemicals using chemistry and process technology conceived in-house, moved through its own pilot plant and engineered to full-scale production. It sells through three business models - Large Scale Manufacturing of proprietary intermediates, Contract/Exclusive Manufacturing for large pharmaceutical and chemical customers under long-term relationships, and Contract Research & Manufacturing Services. Customers are global innovators across pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, oil & gas and material science, with named partners including Milliken, Baker Hughes, SEQENS Group, Saudi Aramco Technologies, Novoloop and Polaroid.

Contract / Exclusive Manufacturing (CEM): Dedicated Baker Hughes product stream at Site 4
Strategic product manufactured exclusively for Milliken & Co. (USA) at Site 3++
Under development: Electronic chemicals for the semiconductor sector

currentContext.strategies: Shift the revenue mix decisively toward contract-led models - CEM plus CRAMS crossed 55% of FY2025-26 revenue (CEM alone 46.3%, the largest business model for the first time) and is targeted at around 70% over the medium term / a majority of revenues by FY2030.|Build capacity ahead of demand at named sites: commission Site 3++ (done, end-February 2026, exclusive Milliken manufacturing), ramp Site 4 for Baker Hughes in the oil & gas vertical, and phase-commission Site 5 at GIDC Panoli starting with the first two production blocks.|Enter semiconductor-linked chemistries through a dedicated semiconductor-materials line at Site 5 (targeted ~400 tonnes) and an electronic-chemicals launch aimed at Japan, Korea and Taiwan.|Sustain R&D as the moat - Rs 862 million (7.3% of revenue) invested in FY2025-26, interim upgrades including additional fume hoods and a new 400 MHz NMR, and a ground-up next-generation R&D facility of 15 laboratories and ~120 fume hoods targeted for commissioning by Q2 FY2027-28 to roughly double research capacity.|Deepen proprietary process IP in photochemistry, continuous flow manufacturing, catalysis and fluorination chemistry to take on more technically demanding projects and defend cost and quality against intensifying global competition.|Institutionalise knowledge - structured knowledge-capture frameworks, cross-site documentation of process learnings and formal R&D-to-manufacturing technology transfer, so expertise survives individual departures.|Use digital-first innovation - data analytics, process simulation and predictive modelling to test process parameters virtually before committing pilot-plant time and raw materials, compressing development cycles.|Diversify the revenue base across pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, material sciences and oil & gas to cushion against sector-specific cyclicality; pharma+agrochem fell to 46% of revenue.|Structure contracts for visibility - long-term, take-or-pay style CEM arrangements that improve revenue visibility and reduce spot-market exposure.|Widen the global footprint - serve over 19 countries from the Surat hub, sustain high-value markets (US, Germany, UK, Japan, China) while expanding into Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa, backed by a dedicated Business Development Leader - Europe effective June 2026.|Tighten working capital - the cycle improved to 179 days in FY2025-26, on a clear path to a medium-term target of 160 days by FY2026-27.|Embed sustainability in process design - direct a significant share of process development at reducing solvent intensity, energy consumption and waste, alongside 16 MW and 15 MW captive solar installations and circular-economy practices.|Grow people and safety capability - 1,119 Aetherians, technical and leadership training pipelines, expanded safety training, hazard identification and mock drills across all manufacturing sites.|Expand CSR footprint across education, healthcare, livelihood and skilling, and environmental stewardship, with CSR spend of Rs 34 MM, up 17.24% year on year.
currentContext.expansion: FY2025-26 was a step-change year in Aether's capacity build-out. Manufacturing Site 3++ (GIDC Sachin, Surat) commenced commercial production in late February 2026 and is in ramp-up, dedicated to exclusive manufacturing for Milliken & Co. (USA) under a 10-year agreement. Site 4, operated by wholly owned subsidiary Aether Speciality Chemicals Limited and fully operational since Q3 FY2024-25, ran at roughly 50% capacity utilisation while its revenue grew from about Rs 50 crore to Rs 219 crore, now about 19% of total sales; management expects it to reach peak potential by FY2027-28. The largest greenfield project, Site 5 at GIDC Panoli (Bharuch), completed utilities and the first two Phase 1 production blocks with solvent trials done, and these are set for commercial operations from June 2026, incorporating a dedicated semiconductor-materials line of approximately 400 tonnes; management has clear visibility on eight further manufacturing plants at the site and Phase 2 construction is progressing, with the bulk of the Site 5 investment scheduled to complete within twelve months. An additional 15-acre land parcel at Panoli (Plot 13, referred to as Site 5+) was acquired to extend the expansion runway. On the research side, the existing R&D centre expansion on adjacent land was completed during the year, adding 15 fume hoods and advanced analytical infrastructure including a new 400 MHz NMR machine, while a ground-up next-generation R&D complex of 15 laboratories and around 120 fume hoods is targeted for commissioning by Q2 FY2027-28, effectively doubling research capacity. R&D investment was Rs 862.13 million, 7.3% of revenue. Captive solar generation has been commissioned in stages, with 31 MW of solar capacity being scaled across operating sites including a 15 MW auto-tracker plant used under the Captive Power Producer segment, improving energy security and lowering operating cost intensity. Funding is internal and debt-light by design: capital work-in-progress grew to Rs 5,061.08 million with Rs 5,413.20 million invested during the year and Rs 104.86 million of borrowing cost capitalised against these projects, lifting the Debt-Equity Ratio from 0.08 to 0.18 - which management characterises as the visible signature of the Site 3++ and Site 5 spend rather than balance-sheet stress. FY2026-27 capex guidance is Rs 3,000-3,500 million, largely for Site 5 and further R&D expansion, and management expects operating cash flow to absorb remaining capital commitments in FY2028 so the Debt-Equity Ratio trends back down. Overall manufacturing utilisation across facilities was about 65% in FY2025-26, leaving headroom alongside the new capacity.

risks.risk: Process-safety and fire exposure across chemical sites and third-party storage
risks.note: Two fire events are disclosed in successive cycles: the November 2023 incident at Manufacturing Facility 2 (now restored and operational, insurance claim still advancing) and a March 2026 fire at an external warehouse in Hojiwala Industrial Estate that originated from neighbouring premises. The March 2026 event caused no injuries and no production disruption but an inventory loss of approximately Rs 70 million was recognised, with an insurance claim lodged and under assessment, and Q4 FY2025-26 earnings absorbed the one-off. Aether also relies on nine external warehouses in Surat, so a share of finished-goods and raw-material value sits in premises it does not control.

risks.risk: Customer and contract concentration in the CEM franchise
risks.note: The pivot that drives margin also concentrates it. Site 4 is dedicated to a single customer, Baker Hughes, and alone contributed about 19% of total sales; Site 3++ was built to manufacture one strategic product exclusively for Milliken under a 10-year sole-partner agreement. CEM is now the largest business model at 46.3% of revenue. Loss, renegotiation or de-validation of any one marquee account would strand purpose-built capacity that has no obvious alternative use.

BRSR Section A records 100% of turnover from one activity, manufacturing of chemicals (NIC 2011), and all five plants are national with no international manufacturing. The manufacturing base, the R&D centres and the pilot plant are clustered in Gujarat across Sachin/Surat and GIDC Panoli, Bharuch, so a regional disruption - regulatory, utility, monsoon, pollution-control-board or local incident - would hit substantially the whole asset base at once.

risks.risk: Execution and absorption risk on a large, concurrent capital programme, with leverage rising to fund it
risks.note: Site 5 (Magnum, Panoli) is the largest greenfield project with only the first two of ten planned production blocks readied, Site 3++ is still in ramp-up, and a next-generation R&D complex is under construction, with FY2026-27 capex guidance of Rs 3,000-3,500 million on top of Rs 3,347.77 million of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account as at 31 March 2026. Debt-equity moved from 0.08 to 0.18 and the current ratio eased from 3.25x to 1.78x. Facilities ran at only about 65% utilisation overall and Site 4 at about 50%, so slipping commissioning dates or slower customer qualification would leave depreciation and interest running ahead of the revenue meant to absorb them.

risks.risk: Pricing pressure in Large Scale Manufacturing, end-market cyclicality and geopolitical disruption
risks.note: Management explicitly flags maintaining margin discipline amid competitive pricing pressure in LSM, which still contributes 43.2% of revenue and had absorbed unprecedented pricing pressure before recovering. Product diversification projects were initiated specifically in light of the agrochemical slowdown during the year. The year opened with sweeping global tariffs and closed with escalating Middle East conflict, and the company sells into over 19 countries, so export realisations and freight remain exposed to trade and conflict shocks.

risks.risk: Climate transition risk from fossil-fuel dependency in manufacturing utilities
risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table identifies high dependency on fossil-fuel utilities inside chemical manufacturing grids as a transition risk under expanding carbon pricing frameworks - a risk and opportunity with both positive and negative financial implications, since mitigation itself requires capital expenditure for solar assets. Mitigation rests on scaling 31 MW of solar capacity across operating sites and commercialising the Converge platform, which traps up to 40% CO2 by weight in polyol manufacturing.

risks.risk: Effluent and hazardous-waste compliance in specialty chemical synthesis
risks.note: Two separate BRSR material issues. Production generates highly concentrated industrial wastewater against stringent local Pollution Control Board rules that demand flawless zero-liquid-discharge discipline; the mitigation - moving completely off groundwater plus MVR-based ZLD and a Soil Biotechnology plant - itself carries a negative financial implication through parasitic power loads and higher monthly utility spend. Separately, synthesis inherently generates by-products and chemical waste subject to tight hazardous-waste regulation including mandatory 180-day storage caps, mitigated through a captive Solvent Recovery Plant. Any lapse is a regulatory-shutdown risk, not merely a cost.

risks.risk: Cyber-security and protection of proprietary process intellectual property
risks.note: The BRSR identifies data privacy and cyber-security integrity as a material risk: migration to paperless corporate networks and remote operational cloud servers opens vulnerabilities to proprietary intellectual property theft and cyber-attack. Because Aether's moat is an accumulated library of in-house process routes and trade secrets rather than patents alone, IP loss would erode the core of the CRAMS and LSM franchises. Mitigation is an Information and Cyber-Security architecture audited annually by third parties against ISO 27001, with ongoing licensing and maintenance outflows flagged as a negative financial implication.

themes.title: Import-substitution / China+1 specialty chemicals
themes.need: After the worst agrochem/chemicals year in living memory, the cycle is turning on China+1 reshoring and global pigment/dye consolidation. SUDARSCHEM is now #2 global pigment player post-Heubach; SUMICHEM posted record FY26 margins; AETHER/ANURAS/DEEPAKNTR/CLEAN add CRAMS + backward-integration; war-driven RM/freight inflation is being passed through. Q1FY27 shows the reshoring build-out actually landing: HSCL grew consolidated revenue 28% to INR 1,432cr with PAT INR 228cr (+27%) at a 22% EBITDA margin while opening three new value ladders in a single quarter (carbon nanotube 200 MTPA by Q4FY27, super-speciality carbon black 6,000 MTPA by FY28, and India's first commercial anthraquinone/carbazole plant), all self-funded with no incremental debt; TATVA grew revenue 43% YoY and delivered its first commercial-plant-scale semiconductor batch, qualified by the customer and called 'the glaring achievement of the past decade' (though commercialisation is explicitly not before Q4 CY2028); FCL tripled total income to INR 386.72cr (+165%) with Texas capacity nearly doubled to 148,000 MTPA and already running 63% on a single shift, so its next revenue leg needs only USD 1-2mn of capex.
themes.driver: Volume rebound as destocking ends; price hikes sticking; new value-ladder commissioning (HSCL CNT/carbon black) and semiconductor-materials qualification (TATVA).

themes.title: Specialty & agrochem CRAMS
themes.need: Custom-synthesis/CRAMS players with a dominant specialty-chemicals & agrochem-intermediate end-market are tied to the agrochem/specialty-chem capex cycle - not pharma APIs.
themes.driver: Specialty/agrochem custom-synthesis order wins tied to the agrochem/specialty-chem capex cycle.

hero.oneLiner: Aether leveraged geopolitical disruptions to drive >20% pricing gains in its Large-Scale Manufacturing vertical while successfully transitioning toward a high-margin CRAMS/CEM model (55% of revenue) with Site 5 commissioning imminent. Despite Q4 one-offs (fire provision, lack of insurance claim income), the structural shift to complex chemistry and expanded R&D capacity positions the firm for sustained 29-30% EBITDA margins and triple-digit growth in semiconductor materials by 2030.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Aether develops, scales up and manufactures advanced intermediates and specialty chemicals using chemistry and process technology conceived in-house, moved through its own pilot plant and engineered to full-scale production. It sells through three business models - Large Scale Manufacturing of proprietary intermediates, Contract/Exclusive Manufacturing for large pharmaceutical and chemical customers under long-term relationships, and Contract Research & Manufacturing Services. Customers are global innovators across pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, oil & gas and material science, with named partners including Milliken, Baker Hughes, SEQENS Group, Saudi Aramco Technologies, Novoloop and Polaroid.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Accelerating global outsourcing demand - global chemical majors seeking capable, reliable Indian partners to de-risk supply chains, described as a multi-year structural shift.
- China Plus One shift among global chemical and pharmaceutical innovators, plus rising foreign direct investment and government Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, named as macro tailwinds.
- Structurally higher costs in the US and Europe making India a preferred global manufacturing hub, with project timelines compressing to 12-24 months in many cases.
- Mix shift to CEM and CRAMS as the core margin lever - higher-value, relationship-led, recurring, long-tenor revenue with structurally superior economics and better absolute EBITDA per rupee of revenue.
- Pricing strength in Large Scale Manufacturing - product prices up over 20% year on year through most of the year, with a strong pricing recovery in the last two quarters that management expects to sustain.
- Operating leverage from newly commissioned capacity - Site 4 revenue up nearly 4x to Rs 2,196 million (~19% of sales), Site 3++ ramping ahead of schedule, Site 5 blocks readied for June 2026.
- CRAMS pipeline strengthening on niche chemistries, complex synthesis capability and growing enquiry volumes from customers diversifying away from single-geography sourcing; CRAMS programmes are the feedstock for future CEM conversions.
- Energy security as a demand theme - industry reports projecting Asia needing roughly US$5-6 trillion of investment over five years and India US$500-600 billion, against which Aether is advancing multiple CRAM projects.
- Domestic market strength - India contributed 75% of FY2025-26 revenue versus 60.53% in FY2024-25, on LSM pricing and CEM supply to Indian companies; exports and deemed exports contributed nearly 30% of revenue.
- Geopolitical headwinds - global tariffs at the start of the year and Middle East conflict in the final quarter - flagged as disruption but also as reinforcing the premium on India-based partners.
- One-off headwinds absorbed in Q4 FY2025-26: an inventory loss provision from a March 2026 fire at an external warehouse and a logistics-related claim.
- Sustainable process design increasingly a qualifying criterion rather than a differentiator for global customers.
- No order book figure is disclosed; management describes a 'robust project pipeline' underpinning confidence that CEM and CRAMS grow to roughly 70% of revenues.
- Site 5: first two plants on track for Q1 FY2026-27 with 'clear visibility on the subsequent eight manufacturing plants'.
- 10-year exclusive contract manufacturing agreement with Milliken, executed June 2025, making Aether the sole contract manufacturing partner for a key strategic product; commercial operation began at Site 3++ in February 2026.
- Baker Hughes contract ramping at Site 4, with products validated across multiple global facilities and peak potential expected by FY2027-28.
- A fresh CEM contract with a large European multinational in the material science space signed during the year.
- Advanced discussions with several customers evaluating Aether as their preferred partner for globally novel products.
- 19 new marquee clients onboarded and over 50 customer and certification audits completed during FY2025-26.
- Long-term, take-or-pay style supply contracts for niche chemistries in North America (United States and Mexico).
- Three new large-scale pharmaceutical and agrochemical products slated for launch by May/June 2026.
- CRAMS pipeline described as continuing to strengthen, with growing enquiry volumes; CRAMS contributed 9.2% of consolidated revenue.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: FY26 EBITDA margin expanded to 31% from 28%; Q4 margins pressured by INR 70 mn fire provision and INR 10 mn year-end provisions; Open cost-plus P&L for CEM protects against raw material inflation; LSM seeing temporary margin delta from price hikes.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Debt expected to increase sequentially by INR 200-250 mn in FY27 to fund capex; Working capital cycle improved to 179 days (from 194), targeting 160 days by FY27 end; Cash flow from operations up to INR 1,424 mn.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY2025-26 was a step-change year in Aether's capacity build-out. Manufacturing Site 3++ (GIDC Sachin, Surat) commenced commercial production in late February 2026 and is in ramp-up, dedicated to exclusive manufacturing for Milliken & Co. (USA) under a 10-year agreement. Site 4, operated by wholly owned subsidiary Aether Speciality Chemicals Limited and fully operational since Q3 FY2024-25, ran at roughly 50% capacity utilisation while its revenue grew from about Rs 50 crore to Rs 219 crore, now about 19% of total sales; management expects it to reach peak potential by FY2027-28. The largest greenfield project, Site 5 at GIDC Panoli (Bharuch), completed utilities and the first two Phase 1 production blocks with solvent trials done, and these are set for commercial operations from June 2026, incorporating a dedicated semiconductor-materials line of approximately 400 tonnes; management has clear visibility on eight further manufacturing plants at the site and Phase 2 construction is progressing, with the bulk of the Site 5 investment scheduled to complete within twelve months. An additional 15-acre land parcel at Panoli (Plot 13, referred to as Site 5+) was acquired to extend the expansion runway. On the research side, the existing R&D centre expansion on adjacent land was completed during the year, adding 15 fume hoods and advanced analytical infrastructure including a new 400 MHz NMR machine, while a ground-up next-generation R&D complex of 15 laboratories and around 120 fume hoods is targeted for commissioning by Q2 FY2027-28, effectively doubling research capacity. R&D investment was Rs 862.13 million, 7.3% of revenue. Captive solar generation has been commissioned in stages, with 31 MW of solar capacity being scaled across operating sites including a 15 MW auto-tracker plant used under the Captive Power Producer segment, improving energy security and lowering operating cost intensity. Funding is internal and debt-light by design: capital work-in-progress grew to Rs 5,061.08 million with Rs 5,413.20 million invested during the year and Rs 104.86 million of borrowing cost capitalised against these projects, lifting the Debt-Equity Ratio from 0.08 to 0.18 - which management characterises as the visible signature of the Site 3++ and Site 5 spend rather than balance-sheet stress. FY2026-27 capex guidance is Rs 3,000-3,500 million, largely for Site 5 and further R&D expansion, and management expects operating cash flow to absorb remaining capital commitments in FY2028 so the Debt-Equity Ratio trends back down. Overall manufacturing utilisation across facilities was about 65% in FY2025-26, leaving headroom alongside the new capacity.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Highly confident; Emphasizes 'golden age' for Indian specialty chemicals; Focus on execution and scaling complex chemistry; Strategic hiring (ex-Bayer/ALTANA) to open new frontiers in material science.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- In-house R&D as the core engine - every chemistry and technology is conceived, developed and perfected internally, scaled in the company's own pilot plant and engineered to full-scale production
- R&D spend of Rs 862 million in FY2025-26, 7.3% of revenue, described as among the highest in the Indian chemical industry; team organised into 11 specialised research groups
- Existing R&D facility with 55 fume hoods running at peak capacity, ~70% focused on non-pharma and non-agrochemical projects, being augmented with 15 more fume hoods and NMR spectroscopy
- Sticky, long-tenor customer contracts - 10-year exclusive contract manufacturing agreement with Milliken, dedicated Site 4 for Baker Hughes with products validated across multiple global facilities, plus SEQENS, Saudi Aramco Technologies, Novoloop and Polaroid relationships
- Deep customer qualification barrier - more than 50 customer and certification audits and multi-day HSE audits cleared in the year; 19 new marquee customers onboarded
- Versatile manufacturing ecosystem serving three business models (LSM, CEM, CRAMS), which management credits with mitigating sector-specific slowdowns
- Products never before made in India, competing with established Chinese players; import-substitution positioning
- Captive renewable energy (16 MW static plus 15 MW auto-tracker solar) and a captive Solvent Recovery Plant, MVR-based ZLD and Soil Biotechnology plant reducing energy and raw-material cost intensity
- Academic and talent pipeline through tie-ups with NCL Pune, ICT Mumbai, Uka Tarsadia University and SVNIT Surat, including company-sponsored PhD programmes

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Geopolitical volatility affecting feedstock/logistics (though currently beneficial for pricing); Execution risk on Site 5 commissioning; Working capital intensity during ramp-up; Fire incident at external warehouse (INR 70 mn loss).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Management explicitly states geopolitical conflict has driven unprecedented pricing power (>20%) which they believe is sustainable for 2-3 quarters; Shift to selling via Indian subsidiaries of MNCs temporarily reduced direct exports but is reversing; New 'Integrated Polymerizations' competency is a stealth entry into high-barrier oil & gas additives.
